items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that LU factorization involves writing a matrix [MATH: A] as a product of two matrices [MATH: L] and [MATH: U,] where

Content:
- [MATH: [1|0|0; ∗|1|0; ∗|∗|1]] is a unit lower triangular matrix (a lower triangular matrix that has only [MATH: 1]'s on the main diagonal), and
- [MATH: [∗|∗|∗; 0|∗|∗; 0|0|∗]] is an upper triangular matrix.

Content:
For example, suppose we're given the matrix [MATH: [1|− 1|− 2; 0|2|− 3; − 2|2|7]] To perform LU factorization, we need to write [MATH: A] as

Content:
[MATH: [1|− 1|− 2; 0|2|− 3; − 2|2|7]]

Content:
As usual, to find the matrices [MATH: L] and [MATH: U,] we can reduce the matrix [MATH: A] to echelon form while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

Content:
[MATH: A|= [1|− 1|− 2; 0|2|− 3; − 2|2|7]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + 2R_{1}|⇔|[1|0|0; 0|1|0; 2|0|1]^(⏞)^(E_{1}) ⋅ A; ∼[1|− 1|− 2; 0|2|− 3; 0|0|3] = U]

Content:
The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix [MATH: U.] Now, since [MATH: E_1A=U,] we can invert [MATH: E_1] to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

Content:
[MATH: E_{1}A|= U; A|= E_{1}^{− 1}U; A|= [1|0|0; 0|1|0; 2|0|1]^{− 1}U; A|= [1|0|0; 0|1|0; − 2|0|1]_(⏟)_(L)[1|− 1|− 2; 0|2|− 3; 0|0|3]_(⏟)_(U)]

Content:
Caution: In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix [MATH: A] to its echelon form:

Content:
- we can only add multiples of higher rows to lower rows ([MATH: R_j:=R_j+k R_i] where [MATH: i < j]), and
- the other elementary row operations (swapping or multiplying a row by a number) are not allowed.
